## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**It assumes a stall angle.** The 15 degree figure used throughout is an assumption, and every corridor and descent figure scales with it directly. A thick wing with leading edge devices stalls later, and the fraction of the conversion spent stalled moves with it.

**It treats the slipstream as uniform.** Momentum theory gives an average. A real slipstream is non-uniform and differently deflected across the span, and the immersed wing does not see one dynamic pressure. Kirby notes that the simple resolution of velocities is the one obtained with counterrotating propellers, whose slipstream carries no rotation, so the X-18's contra-rotating propellers are the case it describes best and the swirl of a single-rotation propeller is a lesser error here.

**It uses a single representative contraction factor.** The 0.85 is a judgement, and the immersed fraction ranges from 47 to 67 percent across defensible choices, which is a wide band on the article's central quantity.

**It treats the final flight as an aerodynamic event.** In one account it was a propeller pitch control failure and in the other an engine failure. The aerodynamics explain why the consequence was severe and do not explain why the failure occurred, and no public account of the fault exists among the sources cited here.

## The Source Base

**The survey rests on 7,598 research records assembled from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,517 are report primaries, being 20.0 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. 7,339 of the records carry a year, with a median of 2013.

Unlike the two preceding articles, **this subject has a real technical literature**. The tilt-wing was studied intensively by the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics and its successor, and the configuration's design considerations, wind tunnel behaviour, slipstream interference, and handling qualities are all documented in primary sources.

What is scarce is documentation of **this aircraft**. No report in the Technical Reports Server of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration carries the designation in its title, and no X-18 report appears among the Defense Technical Information Center records registered with Crossref. The aircraft's own engineering record is the Hiller report series in the [Lindenbaum collection][ref_lindenbaum_x18], which is on paper only and contains no catalogued report of flight results. The closest published primary documents are Schade's ground-effect measurements on an X-18 model, which cite full-scale X-18 tests, in [NACA 1960, Conference on V/Stol Aircraft a Co][research_naca_1960_2], and the [Air Force history][ref_af_tilt_wing_history]. So the pattern is the inverse of the [X-16][related_post_a313_bell_x16] and [X-17][related_post_a314_lockheed_x17] articles, where the question had a literature and the vehicle did not. **Here the configuration has a literature and the individual airframe does not**, which is a milder version of the same difficulty.

**One retrospective paper on the aircraft itself is on record.** [Nichols 1990][research_nichols_1990] is a conference paper of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics on the lessons learned from the Hiller X-18. Its text is not drawn on here, so the dimensions, dates and flight record above rest on the inventory, the encyclopaedia entry and the Air Force history.

Every dimension and weight is from secondary compilation, and the one weight an official source states independently, the Air Force history's sixteen and a half tons, agrees with it. **The sources disagree on three points**, the first flight date of 20 or 24 November 1959, whether the last flight ended with an engine failure or a propeller pitch control problem, and whether the aircraft's scrapping is documented.

### The Shape of the Reference Base

Of the 7,339 dated research records, **4,432 predate 2019 and 2,907 do not**. The distribution runs 307 documents from before 1960, 1,328 from the 1960s and 1970s, 1,170 from the 1980s and 1990s, 1,627 from 2000 to 2018, and 2,907 from 2019 onward. The contemporary share is large because **the configuration actually returned**, so surveying the present state of it is surveying a live engineering field rather than an epilogue.

**The single most apposite document in the article is the measurement of the descent capability of two-propeller tilt-wing configurations in [Hassell and Kirby 1966][research_james_l_hassell_1966]**, which is the X-18's exact arrangement addressing the X-18's exact difficulty.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when it is a NASA Technical Reports Server url or carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. 1,014 of the records are reports-server urls, and the NACA and NASA tilt-wing, deflected-slipstream, descent and V/STOL handling-qualities reports on which the period argument rests are reached that way, so the rule counts them.

**The rule does not reach the journal and conference literature of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, abbreviated AIAA.** 2,504 of the records carry its 10.2514 prefix, among them the retrospective paper on the X-18 and design and flight test papers written by the people who built the vehicles they describe. The Hiller company reports in the Lindenbaum collection are on paper only and are not in the survey at all. **20.0 percent is therefore a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand.**

### Thin Subjects

**Eight subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the immersed fraction of the span | immersed, immersion | 4 |
| the contraction of the slipstream | contraction, contracting, contracted | 4 |
| the local angle of attack of a blown wing | local angle of attack, local incidence, effective angle of attack | 0 |
| cross-shafting and interconnected drives | cross shaft, interconnect | 6 |
| asymmetric and differential thrust | asymmetric thrust, thrust asymmetry, asymmetric power, differential thrust, differential propeller thrust | 7 |
| the hover figure of merit | figure of merit | 1 |
| the helical tip Mach number | tip mach, helical tip | 8 |
| density altitude and roll authority | density altitude | 1 |

**The keystone has no literature under its own name.** The four titles that carry the word immersed or immersion concern immersion and invariance control, immersed-boundary numerical methods and immersion cooling, and none concerns a wing in a slipstream. The immersed fraction is studied as the slipstream and as propeller and wing interaction in the clusters above, and the article's own figure of 57 percent stands on the geometry and the contraction factor shown in How Much of the Wing Is Immersed.

**The contraction of the slipstream appears in four titles**, [Conway 1998][research_conway_1998], [Iwasaki 1959][research_iwasaki_1959], [Sparks and Miley 1983][research_sparks_miley_1983] and [Theodorsen 1944][research_theodorsen_1944], which is why the contraction range of 0.707 to 1.0 is taken from momentum theory and the 0.85 is reported as a judgement. **No title names the local angle of attack of a blown wing**, so the relation in The Relation That Makes the Configuration Work stands on the resolution of velocities shown there and on Kirby's period treatment of it.

**Cross-shafting has five titles of its own**, two of them on the landing reliability of V/STOL aircraft, [Willis 1980][research_willis_1980] and [Willis 1981][research_willis_1981], and the remaining title that carries interconnection concerns an electrical grid. **The figure of merit appears in one title**, on meshing rotors, so the check of 0.674 rests on momentum theory and the published weight and power, and density altitude appears in one, [Strand and Ennis 2012][research_strand_ennis_2012], so the 26 percent loss of roll authority at ten thousand feet rests on the standard atmosphere. **The helical tip Mach number is a noise subject in these titles**, with seven of its eight records on noise or aural detection.

### What the Survey Admits

**Every research title has been read for relevance, and a record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is a tilted wing in a propeller slipstream and everything the article dimensions to decide whether a conversion exists, from the actuator disc and the propeller at low advance ratio, through the stall of the wing and the devices that delay it, the corridor, descent and the vortex ring state, hover control and handling qualities and engine failure, to the ground environment and the electric successors that inherited the configuration. The tilt-rotor, deflected-slipstream, jet-lift and helicopter literatures are admitted where they treat a quantity the article computes.

**Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded.** Propeller also names the screw of a ship, the runner of a hydro turbine, a current meter, a ventilating fan and a microcontroller, and controllable pitch is very largely a marine subject. Slipstream also names a form of fiction, a mode of program execution and a side stream in a coal gasification plant. Outwash is also a glacial landform and its aquifers, hot gas ingestion is also the ingestion of hot gas into the rim cavity of a turbine, and ground effect machines are air-cushion vehicles. Transition is also the laminar-turbulent transition of a boundary layer, stol is a chair in Danish and a round table in Croatian, the osprey is also a bird and Hiller is also the name of composers, artists and chemists. Standard atmosphere also names radio refraction, room acoustics, the greenhouse effect and the conditioning of test specimens. High angle of attack also names missile aerodynamics, vortex ring also names structures in a methane diffusion flame, disc loading also names the loading of the jaw joint, and certification also names the qualification of welding personnel, nursing credentials and halal certification. The wind tunnel also tests cars, trucks and buildings, and the correlation of tunnel with flight for fixed-wing aircraft outside powered lift is a different problem. Correction, erratum, corrigendum and retraction notices, figure, table and supplementary-file records and journal front matter are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. Reviews of books, dictionary and other reference entries of two pages or fewer, news and other notices, and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and stay.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Wing-in-ground-effect craft and their theory, laboratory hover rigs, and actuator disc theory developed for wind turbines are kept for the ground effect and momentum theory they share with this article. Fixed-wing climb and descent, continuous descent in air traffic management, the fuel flow of an airliner in descent, a vortex ring generated by a microramp and a vortex-ring method for a flapping wing rotor are kept for the descent section, research issues in the transition to free flight and a state transition graph for trajectory optimisation for the transition section, and turbine vane cooling with one engine inoperative for the engine-out section. Aviation certification outside powered lift, machine learning prediction of aerodynamics outside powered lift, the communications and cybersecurity of urban air mobility, the jet-flap interaction noise of airliners, the management of the V-22 programme and propeller titles whose medium the title does not state are kept as the neighbouring field of a section of this article. A reader may weigh each accordingly.

**Because every title has been read, the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** The largest class removed is the marine propeller, because the propeller of a ship shares the vocabulary of pitch, thrust, wake and contra-rotation with the propeller of an aircraft.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact.** The X-18 was built from a Chase YC-122C fuselage with Allison T40 turboprops taken from the XFY-1 and XFV-1 programmes and a Westinghouse J34 in the tail for pitch control. Proposed in 1954, designated in October 1957 and unveiled on 8 December 1958 under Air Force funding. First flight 20 November 1959 in the inventory and 24 November 1959 in the Air Force history, twenty flights, last flight July 1961, fastest 253 miles an hour and highest 35,300 feet. The last flight ended in one account with a propeller pitch control problem during an attempted conversion at ten thousand feet and a spin from which the crew recovered, and in the other with an engine failure. No source records a hover or a completed conversion. The programme was cancelled in January 1964 and the aircraft was cut up for scrap in one account and is generally assumed to have been scrapped in the other. The engines were not cross-linked. The XC-142 followed with four propellers and engines linked so that one could turn all four.

**Engineering analysis, reproducible from the stated inputs.** The local angle of attack relation and its consequence that the immersed panel sits at exactly zero incidence at zero forward speed. The maximum tolerable tilt from 90 degrees at ten metres per second to 30 at sixty. **The conversion corridor, which exists at every speed with a margin between 12.6 and 38.0 degrees of tilt.** The descent rates that close it, from 284 feet per minute at the slow end to 1,349 at the fast end, which are upper bounds because the relation holds the slipstream fixed while a real descent reduces power. The induced velocity falling from 40.05 to 24.71 metres per second across the conversion while slipstream dynamic pressure rises from 2,210 to 5,772 pascals. The advance ratio range of 0 to 1.12 and the helical tip Mach number of 0.844. The aspect ratio of 4.364 against a quoted 4.36. The immersed span fraction of 66.7 percent uncontracted, 47.1 fully contracted, and about 57 at a representative factor. The stalled fraction of the conversion at 83.3 percent. The induced velocity of 40.05 metres per second, disc loading of 82.1 pounds per square foot, and slipstream dynamic pressure equivalent to 117 knots. The immersed lift fractions. The hover power of 7,883 ideal horsepower and the implied figure of merit of 0.674. The engine-out rolling moment of 268 kilonewton metres and the aileron fractions. The tolerable thrust asymmetry figures and the 26 percent authority loss at ten thousand feet. The pitch jet crossover at 59 knots.

**Inference, and clearly labelled.** That the outer wing being stalled is the configuration's defining problem is an inference from the geometry and a stall angle, supported by the period literature on tilt-wing stall but not derived from X-18 flight data. **That a corridor exists at every speed rests on a crude lift model** in which the immersed panel is given a linear lift curve to its stall and the outer panel a constant stalled lift coefficient of 0.6. The shape of the result is robust and the individual margins are not. That the XC-142's four propellers and cross-shafting were responses to the X-18's specific failures is an inference from the design changes and their evident purpose.

**Assumed values.** No source states the following, and each is an assumption of this article. The stall angle of 15 degrees, the contraction factor of 0.85, the part-developed slipstream of 1.5 times the induced velocity at the wing, the immersed panel's lift curve and the stalled outer-panel lift coefficient of 0.6, the propeller's lateral station at a quarter span, the aileron effectiveness of 0.08 per radian at 20 degrees of deflection, the pitch jet's arm of 8.64 metres and deflected thrust of a thousand pounds force, the elevator effectiveness of 1.2 per radian at 20 degrees of deflection, and the propeller speed of 1,100 revolutions per minute.

**What the record does not settle.** Whether the last flight ended with a propeller pitch control failure or an engine failure, and what caused it. Whether the scrapping of the aircraft is documented. Whether the X-18 would have converted successfully had it not been grounded. What immersed fraction the designers believed they had. Whether the aircraft was ever close to a hover.

**The pitch jet crossover rests on an assumed elevator effectiveness.** The crossover of 59 knots uses an elevator effectiveness coefficient of about 1.2 per radian, which is the correct order for an aircraft of this class. The crossover speed varies as the inverse square root of that coefficient, so a value of 0.02 per radian would put it at 454 knots, which is implausible for such an aircraft.

**What the contemporary survey changes.** The contemporary survey is organised by field, and its central observation acts on the article rather than extending it. **The keystone was dissolved rather than solved.** This article spends its length computing an immersed fraction whose value was set by the X-18 having exactly two propellers, and nothing about a tilt-wing requires two. There were two because each needed a turboprop, a gearbox and a propeller, and those were expensive, heavy and unreliable enough that more was not sensible. Electric propulsion removes every one of those reasons, and a distributed arrangement immerses essentially the whole span. **The quantity this article is built on goes to unity, and the problem is deleted rather than answered.**

**Information postdating the editorial date.** The contemporary literature section is written from current knowledge.

## Out of Scope

The XC-142 programme deserves its own treatment and gets a paragraph here. The V-22 and the tilt-rotor line generally are named as the surviving alternative and not analysed. The detailed aerodynamics of swirl in a propeller slipstream are cited rather than derived. No attempt is made to reconstruct the X-18's flight envelope. The vortex ring state, which is the related descent hazard for a lifting rotor and which a tilt-wing can also meet, is not treated.

## Conclusion

The X-18 asked whether a wing could be tilted through ninety degrees and flown all the way. It never found out, and the reason it never found out is contained in the arithmetic of its own geometry.

**Two sixteen-foot propellers on a forty-eight-foot wing immerse a little over half of it.** The immersed part flies at an equivalent 117 knots while the aircraft stands still. **The rest of the wing is stalled for five sixths of the conversion**, and no wing design fixes that, because the wing is pointed away from the air by construction.

That would have been survivable with margin elsewhere. There was none. **The ailerons supply under one percent of the rolling moment an engine failure produces in hover**, the engines were not cross-linked so an engine failure was available to produce it, and a few percent of thrust asymmetry exhausts the roll control during conversion. When a propeller pitch control fault, or in the other account an engine failure, duly appeared, the aircraft departed.

**The configuration was not wrong and this aeroplane was under-equipped for it, and the corridor calculation is what establishes that rather than merely asserting it.** A usable tilt margin exists at every speed, between twelve and thirty-eight degrees, so the tilt-wing is a sound idea that this particular aeroplane could not exploit. The XC-142 answered with twice the propellers along the wing and engines linked so that one could turn them all, which is a list of the X-18's deficiencies written as a specification. **The X-18's contribution was to establish, expensively and at the edge of a fatal accident, what the minimum version of the idea could not do.**
